title: Dolan v. United States Postal Service (2006)
shortTitle: Dolan v. United States Postal Service (2006)
summary: The Supreme Court rejected an expansive reading of the postal-matter exception and allowed a claim concerning mail negligently left on a porch to proceed.
notes: The district court dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, reading the 'negligent transmission' exception to bar physical-injury claims as well as claims for damaged or delayed mail; the Supreme Court (546 U.S. 481, decided February 22, 2006) reasoned that 'negligent transmission' must be read in context with its neighbors 'loss' and 'miscarriage,' which limit it to mail that is lost, damaged, delayed, or delivered to the wrong address.

sections.Parties: Barbara Dolan sought tort damages from the United States Postal Service and the government for a delivery-related injury. The government argued that the Federal Tort Claims Act’s postal-matter exception preserved immunity.
sections.Material Facts: Dolan tripped over mail negligently left on her porch. Her claim depended on alleged negligent placement rather than failure to deliver mail, delivery to the wrong address, delay, or damage to its contents. The Court assumed for the interpretive question that corresponding conduct by a private party would support a claim under applicable state law.
sections.Procedural History: The district court ruled for the government, and the Third Circuit affirmed, disagreeing with Raila and construing ambiguity in favor of immunity. The Supreme Court granted review to address the circuit split, reversed, and remanded. Kennedy wrote for seven Justices, Thomas dissented, and Alito did not participate. The remand did not determine tort liability or damages.
sections.Issue: Did section 2680(b)’s protection for claims arising from loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of postal matter include the alleged porch slip-and-fall?
sections.Holding: No. The exception retained immunity for harms from failures of mail delivery and related damage, rather than all injuries caused during delivery.
sections.Reasoning: The majority accepted that transmission viewed alone could include delivery, but read it with loss and miscarriage, the whole statute, purpose, and precedent. Its associated-words analysis kept the phrase within the class suggested by neighboring terms. Kosak and the acknowledged availability of negligent-driving claims undermined the government’s proposed distinction between injury caused by a parcel and injury caused by a postal truck. The specificity of this exception contrasted with broader exceptions Congress used elsewhere, and registration or insurance could address some of the delivery failures it covered. A general presumption favoring sovereign immunity was unhelpful where overly broad exceptions would defeat the Act’s broad waiver. Thomas would apply the ordinary meaning of transmission through completed delivery. Katzmann emphasizes that Scalia joined the majority, illustrating that interpretive approaches do not divide every case into fixed judicial camps.

topics.lrs-k-noscitur: Loss and miscarriage narrowed the neighboring phrase negligent transmission.
topics.lrs-k-sovereign-immunity: The majority declined to construe an FTCA exception so broadly that it undermined the waiver’s purpose.
topics.lrs-k-textualism: Thomas’s ordinary-meaning account conflicted with the majority’s contextual reading of the same phrase.
topics.lrs-k-statutory-structure: Comparison with other FTCA exceptions helped determine how narrowly Congress delineated postal immunity.
topics.lrs-k-canons: The Court declined to apply the canon that waivers of sovereign immunity are construed narrowly to expand an FTCA exception, and Thomas's dissent shows the competing plain-meaning position.
